General Architecture of a Graphics System

Display Controller/Processor 
❖It is the major component which is responsible for generating a 
representation of an image. 
• As shown in previous figure, it takes input from a CPU (host computer)
• Also, it takes input from external sources such mouse, keyboard, joystick, 
and so on.
❖ Image generation is a multi-stage process, and require a lot of computations.
❖ So, if all the computation is performed by CPU, then it is difficult for CPU to 
perform other tasks of the computer.
❖ Hence, a dedicated computing unit is required to do graphics related tasks 
called Graphics Card.
❖All the graphics related computations are performed by a dedicated system 
unit called Graphics Card.  The Graphics card has its own processing unit 
called Graphics Processing Unit (GPU).
❖ CPU assign any graphics rendering related tasks to Graphics Processing Unit 
(GPU) also known as “Display Controller”.

Video Memory 
❖ The output of display controller is a representation of an image (binary 
format).
❖ Video memory (VRAM) is used to store such binary representation of the 
image. It is generally inbuilt in Graphics Card itself. 
❖ In raster scan system, video memory is also known as “Frame buffer”.

Video Controller 
❖ It converts digital image to analog voltage levels that drives electro-
mechanical arrangements of display system.
❖ The size of the frame buffer is same as that of the no. of picture 
elements/ pixels on a display screen. 
❖ For every location on display screen, there is a dedicated memory 
location in the frame buffer.

Color CRT Monitor
❖The color CRT monitor display colors by using a combination of phosphors.
❖The phosphors are of different colors.
❖There are two popular approaches for producing color displays on a CRT:
▪ Beam Penetration Method
▪ Shadow-Mask Method

Beam-Penetration Method
❖ Used in random-scan monitors.
❖ In this method: two layers of phosphor, red and green are used.

Shadow-Mask Method
❖ Used in Raster-Scan display system
❖ Produce a much wider range of colors than that of beam-penetration 
method.
❖ It is used in the majority of color TVs and monitors.
❖ A shadow mask CRT has 3 phosphor color dots at each pixel position, and 
they are arranged in following ways:

Flat Panel Display

Flat Panel Display
❖The Flat-Panel display refers to a class of video devices that have 
reduced volume, weight and power requirement compared to CRT.
❖ Example: Small T.V. monitor, calculator, pocket video games, laptop 
computers etc.
▪Convert electrical energy to light energy
▪Use optical effect to convert sunlight / 
lights from other sources into graphics 
patterns

LED (Light Emitting Diode)
❖A matrix of diodes is organized to form the pixel positions in the display. 
❖Picture definition is stored in a refresh buffer.
❖Data is read from the refresh buffer and converted to voltage levels that are 
applied to the diodes to produce the light pattern in the display.
❖Gallium arsenide (GaAs), gallium arsenide phosphide (GaAsP) and indium 
arsenide (InAs) devices at HP.

Plasma Display Panel 
❖Plasma 
panels, 
also 
called 
gas-discharge 
displays, are constructed by filling the region 
between two glass plates with a mixture of gases 
that usually includes neon, xenon, and so on. A 
series of vertical conducting ribbons is placed on 
one glass panel, and a set of horizontal plates is 
placed into the other glass panel.
❖ Firing voltages applied to a pair of horizontal 
and vertical conductors cause the gas at the 
intersection of the two conductors to break 
down into a glowing plasma of electrons and 
ions.
❖ Picture definition is stored in a refresh buffer, 
and the firing voltages are applied to refresh the 
pixel positions 60 times per second.

▪Note: Emission of plasma electrons 
/ ions give rise to UV-rays, which 
are actually not visual to our eyes.
▪Each pixel cell is coated with 
phosphor, converting the UV light 
into visible light. Each pixel includes 
red, green, and blue phosphor sub-
pixels 
that 
react 
to 
varying 
intensities of charges and blend to 
create the appropriate colors. 
Plasma Display Panel

3D Display Device
▪Three-dimensional display devices enables 
us to perceive depth information. 
▪Types of 3D-display : passive, active, and 
auto-stereoscopic.
▪ Passive 3D-display device:  It provides 
two slightly different images for each eye 
within each frame. One of these images is 
polarized horizontal while one is polarized 
vertically. 
▪When a viewer wears polarized glasses, 
these images enter through the 
corresponding polarized lens, combining 
the two images and providing the illusion 
of three dimensions.
Fig. 01: Passive 3D-display device

3D Display Device : Active 3D-display
❖ Active 3D displays are a bit more sophisticated 
and require powered LCD glasses.
❖ Active 3D displays quickly flash one image for the 
left eye and one for the right eye. 
❖ Uses Computer Vision approach to find disparity 
followed by depth information.
https://www.sears.com/articles/tvs-electronics/televisions/the-evolution-of-display-technology.html

3D Display Device : Auto-stereoscopic 
3D-display
▪
Auto-stereoscopic, or glasses-free, 3D displays are not widely available, but they are 
thought to be the future. 
▪
Instead of relying on glasses to coordinate left eye and right eye perception, the screen 
itself provides the three-dimensional illusion using a technology known as the 
parallax barrier.
▪
A parallax barrier is a device placed in front of an image source, such as a liquid 
crystal display, to allow it to show a stereoscopic or multi-scopic image without the 
need for the viewer to wear 3D glasses.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallax_barrier
